clue.text: Disregard festival

blocks.note: first meaning: to skip or ignore, as a phrasal verb
second meaning: the Jewish spring festival

explanation.walkthrough: Read as two words the answer is a verb for ignoring; read as one it is the Jewish festival marking the Exodus.
explanation.definitionFit: To pass over something is to leave it out, and Passover is the Jewish feast commemorating the Exodus from Egypt.

clue.text: Europeans wanting a divorce, having nothing in common

blocks.note: people from Poland
a couple wanting a divorce wish to live separately

explanation.surface: A European couple, incompatible in every way, seek to split up.
explanation.definitionFit: Two things poles apart are at opposite extremes, as far apart as the North and South Poles, so share nothing.

clue.text: Italian lady in sarong? I must be wrong

indicators.note: if the letters are wrong as they stand, they must be put into a different order

blocks.note: the fodder letters

explanation.surface: An Italian woman wearing a sarong? Surely I am mistaken.
explanation.definitionFit: Signora is the Italian title for a married woman, the equivalent of Mrs or madam.

clue.text: Friendly Greek postman's new round at home

indicators.note: something made new is remade, so these letters are arranged afresh
to go round something is to surround it, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: the fodder letters, including the S
someone at home is in

explanation.surface: A Greek postman doing a new round is on good terms with those at home.
explanation.definitionFit: People on speaking terms are friendly enough to talk to one another.

clue.text: Danes leap daringly from walkway

indicators.note: doing something daringly means wild abandon, so the letters are thrown about

blocks.note: the fodder letters

explanation.surface: Bold Danish holidaymakers jump off the seafront promenade.
explanation.definitionFit: An esplanade is a level paved promenade, usually by the sea, for people to stroll along.

clue.text: I step back taking in face of constantly frozen peak

indicators.note: going back means the word step is read from its end to its start
the face of a word is its front, so only its opening letter is kept
to take something in is to hold it inside, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: taken as written
a pace is a single step
the opening letter of constantly

explanation.surface: A climber edges backwards, gripping the face of a permanently frozen summit.
explanation.walkthrough: I and the reversed step make I-ECAP, which takes the C in just after the I.
explanation.definitionFit: An ice cap is a permanent covering of ice on high ground or a polar region, loosely a frozen summit.

clue.text: Awfully insane compiler's offence

indicators.note: done awfully means done badly, so the letters come out in a wrong order

blocks.note: the fodder letters, including the S

explanation.surface: A crazed crossword setter commits a terrible misdeed.
explanation.walkthrough: Crime passionnel is French for a crime of passion, typically one driven by sexual jealousy.
explanation.definitionFit: A crime passionnel is an unlawful act, usually violent, committed in a fit of jealous passion.

clue.text: Cold, silent, ugly customers

indicators.note: an ugly arrangement is misshapen, so the letters are distorted into another order

blocks.note: C for cold, as on a tap
the fodder letters

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper describes some frosty, wordless and unpleasant patrons.
explanation.definitionFit: Clients are those who buy goods or services from a business, that is, its customers.

clue.text: Left-wing, like the Financial Times?

blocks.note: first meaning: mildly socialist, a paler shade of red
second meaning: the colour of the paper the Financial Times is printed on

explanation.walkthrough: The surface hints at the politics of a business newspaper; the second sense is simply the colour of its newsprint.
explanation.definitionFit: Moderate left-wingers are called pinkos, and the Financial Times is famously printed on salmon-coloured paper.

clue.text: Set up to sell game

indicators.note: in a down clue, setting a word up makes it read from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: to flog is informal British for to sell

explanation.surface: Someone is framed into selling a game.
explanation.walkthrough: Flog is British slang for sell.
explanation.definitionFit: Golf is a sport in which a ball is struck with clubs into a series of holes.

clue.text: On a limb

blocks.note: first meaning: in cricket the on side is also called the ... side
second meaning: one of the body's lower limbs

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests 'out on a limb'; in cricket, the half of the field behind the batter's legs is called both 'on' and 'leg'.
explanation.definitionFit: Cricket uses 'leg' and 'on' interchangeably for one side of the field, and a leg is a limb of the body.

clue.text: Drink situation is conjecture

blocks.note: to sup is to drink in small mouthfuls
a position is a situation or circumstance

explanation.surface: Someone's drinking habits become the subject of idle speculation.
explanation.definitionFit: A supposition is an assumption made without proof, which is what a conjecture is.

clue.text: Game from E Sussex town eaten by mum, boy and girl

indicators.note: what is eaten ends up inside the eater, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: mum, as in 'keep mum', is an instruction to be quiet
Hove is a seaside town beside Brighton in East Sussex
a short boy's name
a girl's name

explanation.surface: A family of three gobble up a seaside town and turn it into a pastime.
explanation.walkthrough: Mum here is the call for silence, not a mother. A halfpenny was an old British coin worth half a penny.
explanation.definitionFit: Shove-halfpenny is a British pub game in which coins are pushed along a marked board.

clue.text: Legendary couple almost decided against plunging into river

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
whatever plunges into something ends up within it

blocks.note: adamant means firmly decided, unshakeable
the Dee is a river in Scotland, and another runs through Wales and Chester
v for versus, meaning against

explanation.surface: A famous pair who all but decided against diving into a river.
explanation.definitionFit: Adam and Eve are the first man and woman in the Genesis story, the archetypal couple of legend.

clue.text: A practical joke, parking on place reserved for taxis

indicators.note: in an across clue one thing placed on another is written in front of it

blocks.note: P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking
a taxi rank is where cabs wait for fares

explanation.surface: Someone thinks it hilarious to park their car in the taxi rank.
explanation.definitionFit: A prank is a mischievous trick played on someone, the same as a practical joke.

clue.text: Article, very gently lifted, is valued

blocks.note: the indefinite article
pianissimo, the musical marking for very soft
raised means lifted up

explanation.surface: An antique, carefully lifted from its place, is assessed by an expert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very gently' is musical shorthand: pp, pianissimo, means play very softly.
explanation.definitionFit: To appraise something is to set a price on it, so appraised means valued in the sense of priced.

clue.text: A 'Cape' trip arranged for each person

indicators.note: things arranged are put into a new order, so the letters are reordered

blocks.note: the fodder letters

explanation.surface: A trip to the Cape is organised for every traveller.
explanation.definitionFit: Per capita is Latin for 'by heads', used to mean for each individual.

clue.text: Mysterious count, rare storyteller

indicators.note: something mysterious is obscure and puzzling, so the following letters are muddled out of order

blocks.note: the fodder letters

explanation.surface: A mysterious aristocrat holds his audience with unusual tales.
explanation.definitionFit: A raconteur is a person who tells anecdotes skilfully, a practised spinner of stories.

clue.text: Photograph showing miss in competition

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it

blocks.note: a cup is a knockout competition, such as the FA Cup
to lose a chance is to miss it

explanation.surface: A photo captures a contestant losing out in a contest.
explanation.definitionFit: A close-up is a photograph taken at short range, showing its subject in fine detail.

clue.text: Power shown by second eleven?

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for second
a cricket or football side has eleven players

explanation.surface: The reserve side show plenty of drive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second eleven' looks like a reserve team, but second and eleven are separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Steam is the energy that drives engines, as in 'run out of steam', so it serves as power.

clue.text: Engulf one climbing across Greek steamship

indicators.note: in a down clue, climbing means reading from the bottom up
lying across something means spanning it, so one piece wraps around the other

blocks.note: taken as written
Gr is the abbreviation for Greek
SS is the abbreviation for steamship

explanation.surface: A wave overwhelms someone clambering over a Greek steamer.
explanation.definitionFit: To engross means to absorb wholly, as when a task swallows up someone's attention.

clue.text: Former county bridge player given small glamorous part

blocks.note: the four bridge players are named North, East, South and West
glam is the shortened form of glamorous
an organ is a part of the body

explanation.surface: A bridge player from a defunct county lands a small but glamorous role.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small glamorous' means the short form of the word, not a minor star; 'part' is a body part, not a role.
explanation.definitionFit: South Glamorgan was a Welsh county, including Cardiff, abolished in the 1996 local government reorganisation.

clue.text: Impress Rex during chat

indicators.note: something happening during an event takes place within it

blocks.note: gab is idle talk
R for Rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: Someone makes a good impression on Rex while chatting.
explanation.walkthrough: Rex, abbreviated R, is the king in royal signatures.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that grabs you appeals to you, as in 'how does that grab you?', so it impresses.

clue.text: Kill to support very bad habit

indicators.note: in a down clue the supporting piece sits beneath, so it is written after

blocks.note: V is the abbreviation for very
to ice someone is slang for to kill them

explanation.surface: Killing to prop up a terrible addiction.
explanation.definitionFit: A vice is an immoral or harmful habit, such as smoking or gambling.

clue.text: Bar in it? One, I suspect, leading one to drunkenness

indicators.note: as an adjective suspect means dubious or unsound, so the preceding letters are not in a trustworthy order

blocks.note: the fodder letters

explanation.surface: Someone eyes a pub and suspects it will lead them straight to drunkenness.
explanation.definitionFit: Inebriation is the state of being intoxicated by alcohol, the same condition as drunkenness.

clue.text: Be in debt to some ne'er-do-well

indicators.note: only some of the following word is wanted, a run of its letters

blocks.note: the run sits across the hyphen in the middle of the phrase

explanation.surface: A good-for-nothing who owes money to everyone.
explanation.definitionFit: To owe someone is to be under an obligation to repay them, which is being in their debt.

clue.text: Former model lay bare

blocks.note: ex means former, as in ex-wife
to pose is to model for an artist

explanation.surface: An ex-model who once posed naked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lay bare' suggests nude modelling, but it is the definition, meaning reveal.
explanation.definitionFit: To expose something is to uncover or reveal it, so it means to lay it bare.

clue.text: Boy is found near the French cathedral city

blocks.note: a boy's name
taken as written
le is French for the

explanation.surface: A lad turns up near a French cathedral city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The French' looks like a description of the city, but it just supplies the French article.
explanation.definitionFit: Carlisle is a city in Cumbria, in north-west England, with a medieval cathedral.
